short_description: An adult Taenia ovis cestode (flatworm) living in a dog's small intestine: ribbon-flat, up to about a metre long, anchored by a scolex bearing four cup-shaped suckers and a rostellum crowned with a double ring of hooks, followed by a short unsegmented neck and a long strobila of proglottids that grow larger and more mature toward the rear. It has NO mouth and NO digestive tract at all — nutrients are absorbed across the tegument. Dogs get it from raw sheep meat; humans are not a host.

morphology_notes: Adult T. ovis lives in the small intestine of dogs and other canids; length commonly 45-110 cm — 'up to about a metre' (WCVM: 'up to 100 cm or more' for dog taeniids).
Ribbon-flat (dorsoventrally flattened) — a tape, not a cylinder. Cream-white to ivory, opalescent; the red/carmine of many micrographs is stain, not the animal's colour.

Scolex: knob-like holdfast head ~1 mm across bearing FOUR cup-shaped muscular suckers (acetabula) arranged radially at roughly 90° spacing, plus an apical rostellum armed with a DOUBLE ring of small hooks (Taenia hook counts overlap between the dog species; the double-row arrangement is the constant, so the render targets 'a double circlet of small hooks', not a specific count). Note: WCVM describes the taeniid rostellum as NON-retractable; the brief's 'retractable' was corrected to follow the source.
Neck: short, narrow, UNSEGMENTED zone directly behind the scolex — the proliferative zone where new proglottids bud; segments are youngest at the front.

Strobila: the long chain of proglottids, each a self-contained hermaphroditic reproductive unit; maturation gradient runs front→rear: immature (wider than long) → mature (roughly square) → gravid (longer than wide, packed with eggs). Gravid terminal segments detach and are passed.

Segment boundaries run TRANSVERSELY — crisp creases ACROSS the width of the ribbon, like rectangles joined end to end. (Repeating-pattern axis trap: the model must not draw lengthwise stripes instead.)

NO mouth, NO digestive tract at any life stage — nutrition is absorbed across the tegument, whose surface is covered in microtriches (microvillus-like projections) that hugely increase absorptive area.

Life cycle: two hosts. Dog = definitive host (adult worm); sheep/goat = intermediate host (Cysticercus ovis, 'sheep measles', cysts in heart/diaphragm/skeletal muscle). Dogs are infected by eating raw, cyst-bearing sheep meat. HUMANS ARE NOT A HOST for T. ovis (unlike T. saginata / T. solium).
Dealt with: a dewormer from the vet (praziquantel) removes the adult worm reliably; not feeding raw sheep carcass meat or offal breaks the cycle.
Whole-worm framing is impossible at 1080²: compose the scolex prominently (~⅓ of frame) with the segmented strobila trailing diagonally out of frame — honest, and shows both diagnostic features.
do_not_draw: Suckers or hooks drawn as rays/spokes radiating from a hub (the starburst trap) — describe the suckers positively as four separate cup-shaped depressions like suction cups on a plunger head, seen at a three-quarter angle so they read as individual cups.
A mouth, jaws, teeth, eyes, or any face on the scolex — the hooks and suckers are attachment organs, not feeding parts; the worm has no mouth at all.
A digestive tract inside the worm (no gut tube in any cutaway).
A cylindrical, round-bodied worm (that is a nematode like the heartworm) — the body is a flat ribbon/tape.
Lengthwise stripes instead of transverse segment boundaries — segment creases run ACROSS the ribbon.
An earthworm-style clitellum or annelid rings on a round body.
Blood, wounds, gore, or a sick/distressed dog — pet-pathogen subject in a children's atlas; show how it is dealt with, not the harm.
Humans as a host — T. ovis does not infect people.

reference.what_it_shows: A single stained scolex, apex up: the rostellum with its double crown of dark recurved hooks clearly resolved and countable, and four circular suckers (all four visible in the whole-mount plane) on the widening head below.
